title: My Calendar I
prompt: Design a `MyCalendar` class to track events without any double booking. A double booking happens when two events have some non-empty intersection (i.e. some moment is common to both events). Implement `book(start, end)`, which represents an event occurring during the half-open interval `[start, end)`. Return `True` if the event can be added to the calendar without causing a double booking, and add it to the calendar; otherwise return `False` and do not add it.

examples.input: book(10, 20) -> true, book(15, 25) -> false, book(20, 30) -> true
examples.explanation: [10,20) and [15,25) overlap at [15,20), so the second booking is rejected. [20,30) does not overlap [10,20) since intervals are half-open, so it succeeds.
The very first booking on an empty calendar always succeeds, since there's nothing yet to conflict with.
Booking the exact same interval twice rejects the second attempt, since it fully overlaps the first.

constraints: at most 1000 calls will be made to book
hints: For each new booking, you need to check it against every previously booked interval for overlap — think about what condition makes two half-open intervals NOT overlap.
Two intervals [s1, e1) and [s2, e2) do NOT overlap exactly when e1 <= s2 or e2 <= s1. Negate that to detect a conflict.

Keeping bookings in a sorted structure (like a sorted list or balanced BST) lets you binary search for the insertion point and only check the immediate neighbors, but a simple linear scan through stored bookings is a fine, simpler solution given the small call limit.

solution.approach: Maintain a list of already-booked (start, end) intervals. To book a new event, check it against every existing booking: two half-open intervals [s1, e1) and [s2, e2) fail to overlap exactly when e1 <= s2 or e2 <= s1, so overlap is the negation of that. If the new interval overlaps any existing booking, reject it; otherwise, add it to the list and accept. Given the constraint of at most 1000 calls, the O(n) scan per booking (O(n^2) total) is efficient enough, though a sorted-container approach could achieve O(log n) per booking.
solution.timeComplexity: O(n) per booking, O(n^2) overall for n calls
